messages.subject: Multivariate probit models in INLA?
messages.subject_clean: Multivariate probit models in INLA?
messages.body_plain:
I've been thinking about trying to fit multivariate probit models in INLA, and whilst I think I have a solution, it looks a bit messy. So I'd appreciate any suggestions on doing better.

The tl:dr question is, probably, can I fix the diagonal terms of the covariance matrix in a Wishart model (e.g. f(idx, model="iid3d"), n=N))?

The problem is where we have multiple binary responses (e.g. we observe the presence/absence of several species at a lot of sites), so our response is a matrix with elements y_ij, for species j in site i, and we also have several covariates, x_ik. If we assumed the species were (conditionally) independent with a linear predictor m_ij = \sum \beta_k x_ik, then we can assume

y_ij ~ Benoulli(p_ij) and probit(p_ij) = m_ij

So far this is just a standard GLM with a probit link. But the observations at a site may not be correlated (e.g. species may tend to co-occur, or competition may keep mean we see one species or another but not both). So we want some sort of residual correlation. The multivariate probit approach does this in a sneaky way. We can re-interpret a probit model as a threshold model: we have a latent variable:

l_ij ~ N(m_ij, 1)

and if y_ij = 1 if l_ij > 0. (if l_ij follows a logistic distribution, then this would be equivalent to a logit link). Now, the extension is straightforward, if L_i is the vector {l_ij} and M_i = {m_ij},  then

L_i ~ MVN(M_i, C)

where C is a correlation matrix, i.e. the diagonal terms are all fixed to be 1. The problem is how to implement this in INLA. If we had a continuous response then this would be straightforward, using a Wishart prior (assuming we don't have too many species!). But I can't see how to do it easily with a binary response. My current approach (see the code below) is to fit a model with C = V + I where V is a covariance matrix and I is an identity matrix, i.e. I have a MVN term in the linear predictor and then fit a univariate model:

form.multi <- Presence ~ Species*(Env1+Env2) + f(site, model=paste0("iid",Nspp,"d"), n=NObs)
multi.inla = inla(form.multi, data = Data, family="binomial",  control.family = list(link = "probit"), Ntrials=1)

The terms in the latent variable have variance diag(v) + 1, so I will have to transform the parameter estimates back to the correct scale, by dividing by diag(v) + 1. I'm a bit worried about ignoring the uncertainty in diag(v) if I do this. One solution would be to fix the diagonal terms (i.e. variances) to a large constant. Can this be done, and if not is there another approach that might work?

Some example code is below:

library(INLA)
library(MASS)

### simulate data
Nspp <- 4
NObs <- 1000

set.seed(94)
# Parameters
Pars <- cbind(
  Intercept = rnorm(Nspp,0,0.3),
  Env1 = rnorm(Nspp,0,0.2),
  Env2 = rnorm(Nspp,0.4,0.3)
)

# Environmental covariates
Covars <- cbind(
  Int <- rep(1,NObs),
  Env1=rnorm(NObs),
  Env2=rnorm(NObs)
)
# Presence/absence data
corr <- 0.5
e.eta <- Covars%*%t(Pars)
Sigma <- corr+diag(1-corr,Nspp)
Pres <- t(apply(e.eta, 1, function(expt, sigma, N) as.numeric(mvrnorm(1, mu=expt, sigma)>0), sigma=Sigma, N=Nspp))
# out it all together
Data <- data.frame(
  Presence = c(Pres),
  Species = factor(rep(1:Nspp, times=NObs)),
  site=rep(1:NObs, Nspp),
  Env1 = rep(Covars[,"Env1"], Nspp),
  Env2 = rep(Covars[,"Env2"], Nspp)
)

# fit univaraite then multivariate probit models
form.univ <- Presence ~ Species*(Env1+Env2)
univ.inla = inla(form.univ, data = Data, family="binomial",  control.family = list(link = "probit"), Ntrials=1)
summary(univ.inla)

form.multi <- Presence ~ Species*(Env1+Env2) + f(site, model=paste0("iid",Nspp,"d"), n=NObs)
multi.inla = inla(form.multi, data = Data, family="binomial",  control.family = list(link = "probit"), Ntrials=1)
summary(multi.inla)

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Is there an Algorithms or Architecture paper for R-INLA?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I know that this is a "cold" thread but I would like to share some thoughts on this. We have done some work to fit unimplemented models in R-INLA by fitting several models with R-INLA where some parameters had been fixed (so that the model could be fitted with R-INLA) and then combining all the resulting models using Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA).

The idea is that if we have a model that is not implemented in R-INLA but that could be fitted by fixing one or a few parameters, then we could take different values of this ensemble of parameters over a grid, fit the conditional models (on the values of these parameters) and then combine them together using BMA. If the model is already available in R-INLA it may be faster to run simpler models and then combine them, depending on the amount of data we have.

I am not sure if this would qualify as a Map-Reduce algorithm. The Map part would be splitting the whole model into (simpler) conditional models and the Reduce step would be to put all the model outputs together to get the desired (and more complex) model.

We have some code in the INLABMA that could me summarised as:

#Define grid on nuisance parameter rho
rrho<-seq(0, .95, length.out=40)

#Fit condintioned models by fixing the value of rho
#sem.inla() uses RINLA to fit a model given the value of rho
#MAP step (?)

 seminla<-mclapply(rrho, function(rho){
                          sem.inla(form, d=columbus, W=W, rho=rho, ...)
     })

#Put all the models together to get our original model
#REDUCE step (?)
sembma<-INLABMA(seminla, rrho, 0)

Conditional models are fitted in parallel using mclapply(). If data are distributed over different nodes, I do not think this approach could handle it, but it could deal with large datasets in one node because we are fitting simpler models. Combining the models only involves computing a weighted sum of matrices (e.g., the matrices representing the posterior marginals) and it can also be done very fast and in parallel.

Not sure if this makes sense, but any comments on this are welcome.

Best,

Virgilio

P.S: This approach is detailed in Bivand et al. (2014), Spatial Statistics journal. You can also check the INLABMA package to get the full example that I have mentioned.

Hi Virgilio,
That's a really cool idea, but I don't think it's exactly the type of thing he's looking for.  The single instances of INLA still wouldn't survive such a large dataset (although it's not impossible to implement it so that it does, depending on how nice SPARK is for linear algebra).

But if the interest is in logistic regression for "tall data", Chopin and Ridgeway wrote a really interesting paper that outlines exactly what INLA is for this special case (as well as a bunch of other algorithms).  They found that Expectation Propogation is the best solution in this case.  (It will be different for more complicated situations, where there are random or mixed effects, but for pure logistic regression, EP looks unbeatable).

Hope this helps,

Dan

n <- 100

stat <- bias <- rep(NA, length(b0))

               control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE))
     e.mean <- exp(r$summary.fix[1,1]+r$summary.fix[2,1]*x)
     mean.e <- r$summary.fitted.val$mean
     bias[k] <- mean(e.mean/mean.e)
  }

plot(b0, bias)  ### or plot(stat, bias)

This figure shows that the bias is higher for smaller counts.

> > > > method from the papers but I am at a disadvantage, being a computer
> > > > scientist, in understanding the details of the algorithms and their
> > > > implementation. I suspect I will have to read the source code and
> > > > reverse engineer the architecture.
> > > >
> > > > I am interested in building a Bayesian model solver for big data
> > > > sets. To make this concrete, let's start simple with Bayesian linear
> > > > regression with a data set that has ten billion rows and a hundred
> > > > real valuated covariates and ten thousand sparse indicator
> > > > covariates. I just made up this example to given an example that will
> > > > never fit in R. I am interested in studying INLA to see if it can be
> > > > solved with the Map-Reduce paradigm use in Spark, an open source
> > > > distributed computing system. Two areas where there are known
> > > > parallel methods with Map-Reduce algorithms for big data sets are
> > > > numerical linear algebra and convex optimization. I am interested in
> > > > learning how INLA uses linear algebra and if the various optimization
> > > > steps are convex optimization problems. One area that has been very
> > > > useful for big data are randomized numerical linear algebra
> > > > algorithms. These algorithms can invert a nxm matrix in O(n x m x
> > > > log(m)). Being yet another approximation in the algorithms, it is
> > > > unknown how the approximation error would propagate through the

Hi Seth,

Someone else will know more clearly what is going on, but i have been working on the similar models so ill give you my 2 cents

The discretised spde mesh in space or space time (through the Kronecker), in a log Gaussian cox model, are considered integration points in INLA. So the area/volume of these mesh nodes is proportional to the expected number of events or the intensity.

So when paramaterising your y's -  you need zeros for your mesh nodes and ones for you actual data

But for the expect/E part where you have the areas/volumes of your mesh, you have a vector with the volumes of the mesh and zeros for your data locations

Finally your observation matrix has the standard projection from mesh to data, and also a diagonal matrix of 1's for the integration points of your mesh.

 Finn or Dan correct me if i am massively off?

library(INLA)

               f(region,model="iid") +

               f(region.x, x, model = "besag",

   control.compute= list(mlik=TRUE,dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))
